newsitem.title: USA: Cohen says Army sex high-profile, not epidemic.
newsitem.headline: Cohen says Army sex high-profile, not epidemic.

text.p: Defence Secretary Willian Cohen said on Tuesday there was no epidemic of sex harassment or marital cheating in the U.S. military and praised the Pentagon for dealing openly with recent embarrassing cases.

"I'm not worried that it's an epidemic. I think we're going through a period in which this has become very much in high profile," Cohen said of incidents in which male drill sergeants were jailed and senior officers relieved of command.

"I believe, overall, our military is doing an outstanding job; our leaders are doing an outstanding job and we are dealing with the issue in a very proactive and open fashion," he told reporters in response to questions at the Pentagon.

Cohen spoke just after the Army announced the commanding general of its scandal-plagued Aberdeen Proving Ground base in Maryland, Maj. Gen. John Longhouser, was retiring. Defence officials privately confirmed a New York Times report that Longhouser admitted to an adulterous affair.
The newspaper said the affair occurred more than five years ago while Longhouser was separated from his wife.

"We have very high standards that we insist upon for the military... It's another example of someone who failed to measure up to those standards," Cohen said at a joint news conference with visiting British Defence Secretary George Robertson.

Calling the case "unfortunate," he said the general himself decided that he was "in a compromising position" because he was the man who decided when others might face military trials for sex-related offences.

In addition to a scandal involving harassment and rape of women recruits by Army drill sergeants at Aberdeen and other bases, Longhouser became the latest in a recent series of military officers to be relieved of their duties or pressed to leave the service because of alleged martial infidelity.

The Army said last week the brigadier general in charge of its medical operations in the Southeast had been relieved of duty and media reports said it was sparked by allegations of an improper relationship between him and a civilian nurse who cared for his critically ill wife.

Brig. Gen. Stephen Xenakis had been commander of Dwight Eisenhower Army Medical Centre at Fort Gordon, Ga., and oversaw six other Army hospitals in the Southeast and Puerto Rico as the Army's Southeast Regional Medical Commander.

The Navy said last week it had relieved Rear Adm. R. M. Mitchell Jr. of his duties as commander of the Navy Supply Systems Command at Mechanicsburg, Pa., because of allegations of conduct unbecoming an officer. A defence source said he was accused of making advances toward a subordinate.

In a very high-profile case, the Air Force's first woman bomber pilot, Lt. Kelly Flinn, was forced to leave the service last week without the honourable discharge she requested in order to avoid court-martial on charges of adultery, having sex with an enlisted man and lying about the matter.

The Army last month also charged its top enlisted soldier with adultery and assault in a case involving four military women in another major chapter of the sexual harassment scandal that has rocked that service.

The Army is now determining whether it will court-martial Gene McKinney, 46, who carries the venerated military title of Sergeant Major of the Army as the leading member of the service's highest enlisted rank. He has denied the charges.
